newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Mexican-style crises now less likely - Goldman Sachs.
newsitem.headline: Mexican-style crises now less likely - Goldman Sachs.

text.p: A new Latin American financial crisis like the one caused by Mexico's devaluation in 1994 is now less likely, partly due to cannier financial markets, Goldman Sachs's managing director said Tuesday.

Gerald Corrigan, managing director of Goldman Sachs & Co, said in a speech at a bankers' conference in Argentina that financial markets are now less likely to "arbitrarily attribute the problems of one country to other countries, thus reducing the threat of contagion risks."

Mexico's surprise devaluation of its peso sent shockwaves throughout much of Latin America. Argentina was particularly hard-hit -- despite the observations of some analysts who argued that its resemblance to Mexico was limited -- and its financial system suffered severe shocks.
But Corrigan said that Latin American nations and financial market participants are now all "more sensitive to avoiding the preconditions that can trigger a serious sovereign liquidity crisis."
Latin American countries have also buttressed their defenses by adopting more conservative debt management policies, including the lengthening of average debt portfolio maturities, Corrigan said.
"My sense of things suggests to me that the risk of such a crisis, with strong contagion effects, is less today than at the time of the Mexican crisis," he said.
